newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Red tape painful for Russia orphans - adoption group.
newsitem.headline: Red tape painful for Russia orphans - adoption group.

text.p: A Russian group helping people wanting to adopt children here said on Wednesday that thousands of orphans were languishing in squalid state facilities because corrupt officials were looking for easy cash.

"Bureaucrats are hiding children from the official rolls to keep their own 'golden reserve' which they will use for speculation," said Viktor Parshutkin, head of the new Public Foundation for Help in Adopting Orphans, using the Russian word "spekulatsiya", traditionally used for illegal profit.
Parshutkin's group was set up late last year to advise parents -- Russians and foreigners -- wishing to adopt children.
But an official from the Education Ministry, which oversees adoptions in Russia, said the charges were not true.
A U.S. official said there were only isolated instances of corruption and that the number of adopted Russian children being brought to the United States was rising all the time.

Russian legislation on adoption has changed frequently since the Soviet Union fell apart, but the Public Foundation said 60 of the 89 regions of the country now allowed foreigners to adopt Russian children.
It said some 35,000 orphans were registered on the Education Ministry's database as looking for a home, but did not say how old the children were.
Adoptive parents, especially those abroad, usually look for infants or very young children because the youngsters are less institutionalised and will find it easier to adjust to a life abroad.
But Parshutkin told a news conference that the majority of adoptable children were hidden from official rolls.
He said would-be foreign parents often paid $20,000 or $30,000 to adopt a child, but he did not know how much of this money was given to local bureaucrats trafficking in children.
A representative of the Ministry of Education who attended the press conference later angrily branded the charges "rude lies and insinuations" and eventually broke down in tears.
"We can't speak of a 'golden reserve' of children for sale, I've heard about it for the first time today," said Alla Dzugayeva, chief lawyer in the Ministry of Education's rehabilitation department.
"Give us concrete facts and we'll start a legal case, let the information be out in the open. We are accused like this all the time but without a single concrete case."

Rumours abound that babies have been sold from Russia, but facts are hard to come by as both anxious adoptive parents willing to pay and corrupt local officials have little incentive to speak about the practice.
Justice Ministry statistician Irina Andryushechkina said two people were convicted for selling children in Russia last year, while five were sentences for related crimes.
Defending his charges, Parshutkin said the fact that just 35,000 of what he described as Russia's 500,000 orphans were available for adoption suggested someone was profiting from their misery.
"If it wasn't profitable for them, they would open up their doors equally to Russians and foreigners alike and they would work openly, publicly and according to the law," he continued.

Dzugayeva said foreigners had adopted 5,200 Russian children since December 1995, and Russians had adopted 11,000. "To say that Russians are preventing adoptions is ridiculous to say the least," she said.
